title: Deep profiling: GPU kernels, CUDA graphs, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM

header: Date: 2025-06-18; Start: 15:00 UTC; Duration: 75 min; Location: Zoom; Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng), Priya Nair (Saffron ML Platform Lead), Tomiko Sato (Saffron Infra), Ethan Park (Saffron ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Saffron SRE)
summary: Technical deep dive comparing kernel selection and runtime strategies for high-throughput, low-latency LLM inference. Main focus: tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM approaches, CUDA Graph replay benefits/limitations with KV cache, batching strategies, and quantization impacts on throughput and quality. Actionable items agreed: microbenchmarks on customer model, share security docs, and run integrated pilot with VPC on-prem preview.
transcript:
00:00 Maya: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intro I'm Maya with Redwood, Diego and Ravi are with me from engineering. can we do a quick round robin?
00:15 Priya: hi this is Priya, ML Platform lead at Saffron. we own the model infra and latency SLOs. Tomiko, Ethan and Liam are also on.
00:34 Diego: great, we'll jump into profiling results and then map to your constraints. quick note — audio may be a bit fuzzy, apologies for any mis-transcripts.
01:05 Diego: high-level, two runtimes we benchmarked: TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) optimized kernels and vLLM style batching scheduler. we ran across A100 and L4 configs. main axes: tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, memory usage, and quality (perplexity and chosen sample evals).
01:40 Priya: our primary worry is p95 < 600ms for 512 token prefix for interactive assistant. throughput also needs to hit 30 concurrent streams.
02:05 Ravi: i'll surface the per-token traces later — the dashboard will show where kernel launch vs matmul dominates.
02:22 Diego: starting with kernel selection: TRT picks fused attention + matmul kernels using Tensor Cores when sequence length and head dims align; that wins for long contiguous decode on FP16/INT8. vLLM relies on cuBLAS/cuDNN and custom attention kernels but uses dynamic batching to pack short requests into larger matmuls.
02:58 Ethan: can you explain how KV cache interacts with CUDA graphs? we tried enabling CUDA graphs and saw some regressions for bursty traffic.
03:20 Diego: yeah — key point: CUDA graphs capture a static sequence of GPU ops and replay them; they need consistent memory addresses for KV cache buffers. when requests vary a lot or the KV grows unpredictably, you get graph mismatch or need to replay with new graphs which incurs overhead. so benefit is big for stable batch shapes, less for highly variable workloads.
04:05 Tomiko: hmm that matches our runs — 10% improvement sometimes, but spikes where latency jumps. any mitigation?
04:24 Diego: two mitigations we discussed: 1) graph specialization per shape bucket and cheap fallback path for mismatches, 2) use graph for the core matmuls while keeping KV management flexible (partial graph). both increase code complexity but are workable.
04:56 Maya: also note persistent worker processes that pre-allocate KV buffers reduce address-churn, which helps graphs be reused. that's what our Dedicated flow does.
05:15 Priya: can you quantify the win for int8/trt vs vLLM fp16? we care about end-to-end latencies and quality loss.
05:33 Diego: numbers from the initial bench: for the 70B Llama variant with 512 prompt + generate 128 tokens, TRT-LLM INT8 with calibration gave ~1.8x tokens/sec vs vLLM FP16 on A100 when the workload had long contiguous decodes. p95 latency improved ~30-40ms in steady-state for single-stream. however, random small requests packed by vLLM gave better amortized latency under bursty small requests because batching overhead was lower.
06:12 Ethan: what about micro-batching vs big batching? we saw higher throughput but p95 exploded.
06:26 Diego: yep that's the classic tradeoff. larger batch sizes improve GPU utilization but increase tail latency because slowest element dictates the step. we recommend adaptive batching windows: a short latency-first window (20-50ms), then accumulate up to N tokens or M tokens total. Redwood runtime dynamically tunes this based on observed tail latency.
07:00 Liam: does the runtime support headroom for model quantization artifacts? we have strict QA.
07:12 Ravi: quantization: INT8 and 4-bit reduce memory and increase tokens/sec but can introduce quality regressions. For 4-bit we use GPTQ-style per-channel quant and test on your eval prompt set. we also provide rollback to FP16 for a small sample of requests (canary) to monitor regression.
07:45 Priya: do you have numbers for 4-bit accuracy hit?
07:51 Diego: depends model; for Llama-70B we saw small but measurable increases in perplexity; top-1/chain-of-thought style tasks showed hallucination risk up ~1-2% in our evals. tradeoff: 2-3x throughput for 4-bit vs FP16. INT8 sits in between with much smaller quality delta if calibrated carefully.
08:38 Tomiko: kernel launch overhead — we saw a lot of time in kernel setup for many small kernels. thoughts?
08:50 Diego: yes, kernel fragmentation hurts. TRT fuses ops and reduces launches; vLLM's modular kernels incur more launches. CUDA graphs also reduce launch overhead by bundling. Another lever is persistent CUDA streams and launching fewer big fused kernels.
09:20 Maya: there was a question about multi-GPU and NCCL — how does KV cache look across GPUs?
09:30 Diego: multi-GPU gets tricky: you either shard KV across GPUs (memory efficient but needs cross-GPU gathers on attention which costs NCCL bandwidth) or replicate and keep per-GPU KV (higher memory but less comm). For low-latency single-session inference we usually prefer per-GPU replication for speed; for very large sequence lengths we shard. Redwood's default is hybrid: replicate for short sessions, shard when memory pressure crosses threshold.
10:12 Ethan: do you have recommendations for on-prem A100 vs cloud L4?
10:20 Ravi: A100 FP16 excels for big fused kernels; L4 is cost-effective but has weaker Tensor Core throughput — TRT optimizations still help but margins shrink. If you plan many small-concurrency flows, L4 plus vLLM dynamic batching might be better cost/perf.
10:50 Priya: about routing and fallbacks — can Redwood route to a lower-precision model when Dedicated is saturated? we need graceful degradation.
11:05 Maya: yes — runtime policy can route to an INT8 variant or smaller model with explicit fallbacks and tagging so we can audit quality. you can define policy by latency, cost, or region.
11:36 Diego: back to CUDA graphs — practical note: warm-up and JIT times matter. first few requests can be slow: graph capture and kernel JIT cause spikes. we recommend a warm-up phase during startup or pre-warm using synthetic inputs. also record that TRT does extra kernel autotuning on first runs that can add 1-2s.
12:15 Liam: how do you measure KV cache hit-rate? that's crucial to our perf.
12:25 Ravi: we log per-request whether prefix found in cache, prefix length matched, and we compute hit-rate windows. on customer traces, hit-rate often is >70% for assistant-type workflows with repeated context; for ephemeral single-turn chat it's lower. tuning cache eviction and prefix canonicalization helps.
13:05 Tomiko: curious about memory fragmentation — we saw OOMs intermittently.
13:12 Diego: fragmentation comes from dynamic allocations for varying batch shapes and kv growth. mitigations: pre-allocate large pools, use slab allocators, and avoid frequent cudaFree. Redwood's Dedicated runtime pins memory and recycles buffers, which reduces fragmentation.
13:50 Priya: can you summarize a recommended config for our SLOs?
13:58 Maya: short answer: A100 dedicated pool + TRT-LLM INT8 for steady long-decode flows; enable graph replay with shape buckets; enable adaptive batching with tight latency windows; fall back to FP16 in canary sampling for quality monitoring; replicate KV for interactive sessions. For bursty, many-small requests, configure vLLM-style dynamic packing on L4 nodes or mixed pool.
14:40 Ethan: any concerns around encryption and KMS with on-prem?
14:47 Ravi: on-prem we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; we can keep control plane in Redwood or deploy control plane privately. data plane and keys can stay in your VPC. we will need to coordinate key rotation windows and offline verification.
15:20 Diego: quick demo link: we uploaded a short bench deck and spreadsheet to the shared drive, link is in chat: https://redwood/saffron/benchmarks (permission required).
15:36 Priya: ok we'll look. for the benchmark you mentioned earlier — please include p99 for 1-2 minute sustained bursts, and error rates.
15:50 Diego: noted. also we'll include per-kernel flame graphs and kernel launch histograms.
16:10 Tomiko: one more — how does TRT-LLM handle variable seq lengths inside a batch?
16:20 Diego: TRT-LLM prefers padded batches with similar seq lengths; you can sort/separate by length into buckets. vLLM packs variable lengths more flexibly but with overhead. so choose bucketization strategy: small number of buckets dramatically improves TRT reuse and reduces padding overhead.
17:05 Maya: okay we're nearing the end, quick recap of agreed pilots: run per-kernel microbench on your model, share prompt set and traffic, Redwood to provide SOC2 + VPC/docs and a pilot plan for on-prem initial install.
17:30 Priya: sounds good. can we get estimated costs for Dedicated A100 pool vs L4 mixed pool?
17:42 Maya: yes we'll share a cost model — Diego and Ravi will include perf assumptions.
17:58 Ethan: thanks everyone, lots to digest.
18:05 Liam: thanks, appreciate the detail.
18:12 Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with notes and the spreadsheet. bye.
18:20 (call ends)
notes: Transcript has occasional mis-hearings and abbreviated technical names; speakers used some shorthand (TRT-LLM, vLLM, A100, L4). Shared artifacts referenced: bench deck (link), benchmark spreadsheet (link), SOC2 summary. We noted graph specialization and KV buffer pinning as key mitigations.
